h1: Who owns your beer label artwork? Copyright and freelance designers
title: Who Owns Your Beer Label Artwork? | Craft Beer School
desc: Copyright in beer label artwork made by freelance designers: who owns it by default in India, why you need a written assignment and what to ask.
teaser: You paid the designer. That does not mean you own the label. In many cases, without the right paperwork, they still do.
standfirst: Many breweries assume that paying for a label means owning it. Under copyright law that is often not true. We explain the basics, the paperwork that protects your brand and the questions to ask before you commission artwork.
sections:
A brewery commissions a freelance illustrator to design a label, pays the invoice and prints thousands of cans. Two years later it wants to use the artwork on merchandise, a new can size or a rebrand. The designer objects, or asks for more money, or has already sold a similar design to someone else.

This happens because copyright in creative work usually belongs to the person who created it, not the person who paid for it. Paying for a design generally gets you permission to use it for the agreed purpose. Ownership is a separate question.
How copyright works for freelance artwork

In India, as in many countries, the creator of an artistic work is generally the first owner of its copyright. There are exceptions, for example for work made by employees as part of their job. Some commissioned works, such as certain photographs, may be treated differently.

For a freelance designer or agency, the safe assumption is: unless there is a written agreement that transfers ownership, the designer may still own the copyright. Indian law expects a transfer of copyright to be in writing and signed. A WhatsApp message saying "it's yours" is not a reliable substitute.

This is general information, not legal advice. Laws change and details matter, so ask a lawyer who handles intellectual property to draft or review your agreements.

There are two main ways to get rights to artwork:

  • Assignment transfers ownership of the copyright to you. You can then use, change and license the artwork as you choose, within what the agreement says.
  • Licence gives you permission to use the artwork in certain ways, for a certain time, in certain places. The designer keeps ownership.

For a beer label that will become part of your brand, an assignment is usually what you want. A licence may suit a one-off limited release or an artist collaboration where the artist wants to keep their work.

Before work starts, agree in writing:

  1. Ownership. Whether copyright is assigned to the brewery and from when (usually on final payment).
  2. Scope. All media and formats: cans, bottles, kegs, merchandise, social media, signage, future pack sizes.
  3. Territory and duration. Worldwide and for the full term of copyright, if it is an assignment.
  4. Source files. Delivery of editable files, fonts used and any licences for stock images or fonts.
  5. Originality. The designer confirms the work is original and does not copy anyone else's.
  6. Moral rights. Creators keep some rights, such as being credited and objecting to distortion. Discuss credit and how the work may be modified.
  7. Portfolio use. Whether the designer can show the work in their portfolio.

Our guide to briefing a design firm covers how to set up the project itself.
Fonts, stock images and AI tools

Labels often include elements the designer did not create. Fonts have licences. Some do not allow commercial packaging use without a paid licence. Stock images have their own terms. Ask the designer to list every font and image used and confirm the licences cover packaging and merchandise.

If a designer uses AI image tools, ask which ones and on what terms. Ownership of AI-generated images is uncertain in many countries. Some tools also have restrictions. For core brand artwork, you want something you can clearly own and protect.

Copyright protects the artwork itself. A trademark protects your brand name and logo as signs of where the beer comes from. A strong label strategy uses both: own the artwork through an assignment, then register key brand elements as trademarks. Our guide to brewery names and trademarks explains the trademark side.

You can only register what you own, so sort out copyright before filing a trademark that includes the artwork.
Fixing it if you already have a problem

If you have labels in use without a written assignment, talk to the designer now, while the relationship is good. Many designers will sign an assignment, sometimes for an additional fee. Waiting until a dispute or a rebrand makes it harder and more expensive.

Keep signed agreements, invoices and final files together, so anyone checking your brand rights later can see the whole picture. Getting this right protects the name and look you are spending years building.
faqs: Do I own a label design I paid for?
Not necessarily. Copyright usually stays with the creator unless there is a written, signed assignment to you. Check your agreement with a lawyer.
What is the difference between assignment and licence?
An assignment transfers ownership of the copyright. A licence only gives permission to use the work in agreed ways while the designer keeps ownership.
Can I trademark a label I do not own?
You should own the artwork before registering it as a trademark. Sort out copyright with the designer first.
